clue.text: State of Britain boosted with a victory song

parts.note: B is a standard abbreviation for Britain or British
taken as written
V for victory
an aria is a solo song in an opera

explanation.surface: A nation's spirits lifted by a triumphant anthem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boosted with' just says the short abbreviation is added to; 'State' is the German Land, not a nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Bavaria is one of the federal Länder of Germany, each of which is officially a state.

clue.text: Retiring party, almost packed

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the last letter of the word for crammed is lost

parts.note: a bash is an informal party
crammed full

explanation.surface: Someone leaving a crowded party early.
explanation.definitionFit: A retiring person is shy and reserved, which is exactly what a bashful one is.

clue.text: Contend with annexe inspection

parts.note: to vie is to compete or contend
a wing is an extension of a building, like an annexe

explanation.surface: Arguing over the survey of a building extension.
explanation.definitionFit: A viewing is an occasion for looking over a property or exhibit, a kind of inspection.

clue.text: Secret royal houses in a past style

indicators.note: the two words house the letters, holding them inside across the gap between them

parts.note: the tail of the first word joined to the start of the second

explanation.surface: A clandestine king lodged in old-fashioned palaces.
explanation.definitionFit: Retro describes design that deliberately imitates fashions from the recent past.

clue.text: Rarity who is excited to be allowed to fly

indicators.note: something excited is agitated and stirred up, so the letters before it are jumbled

parts.note: the nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An unusual person is thrilled to be granted permission to take to the air.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft certified airworthy has been judged safe and so is permitted to take flight.

clue.text: Chap needs a support of course — a 'cow' mainly!

parts.note: a chap is a man
taken as written
on a golf course the ball is supported on a tee

explanation.surface: A man needs some backing, of course, for a woman he calls a cow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mainly' is not 'mostly' but 'of the main', the sea: the animal is a sea cow.
explanation.definitionFit: Manatees are large aquatic herbivores commonly called sea cows, living in the main, an old word for the ocean.

clue.text: Anti-capitalist's sound old currency

indicators.note: sound means the words before it are to be heard, not read, giving a spelling that matches when spoken

parts.note: Karl Marx was the great critic of capitalism

explanation.surface: A revolutionary sounding off about obsolete money.
explanation.definitionFit: The Deutschmark was Germany's money before the euro replaced it, so these coins are a former currency.

clue.text: College intrudes on UK tenant developing Massachusetts resort

indicators.note: something that intrudes pushes its way into the middle of whatever follows
developing means changing form, so the tenant's letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to rearrange
C is a standard abbreviation for college

explanation.surface: A university buys up a British renter's property to build a holiday resort.
explanation.definitionFit: Nantucket is an island off Cape Cod in Massachusetts, a well-known summer holiday destination.

clue.text: What I have here: yarn — not a thing to prick you

indicators.note: not a tells us one letter a is dropped from the story word

parts.note: pointing at something close at hand
a yarn is a story

explanation.surface: Someone showing off some wool and promising it is soft, not prickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'yarn' looks like wool but is a story.
explanation.definitionFit: The thistle is a plant with spiny leaves and stems that scratch anyone who touches it.

clue.text: Aims to keep the French Sabbath going for ever

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so the article sits within the first word

parts.note: aims or goals are ends
le is French for the
S is a dictionary abbreviation for Sabbath

explanation.surface: Plans to keep Sunday observance in France alive in perpetuity.
explanation.definitionFit: Something endless never stops, so it goes on and on without any limit in time.

clue.text: Stew of sheep's head and flounder

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: first letter only
to welter is to roll about or flounder

explanation.surface: A recipe: a broth of mutton head and flatfish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stew' and 'flounder' pose as food, but they are verbs.
explanation.definitionFit: To stew is to suffer oppressive heat, which is what it means to swelter.

clue.text: Career Oscar? Not finalised — go berserk!

indicators.note: not finished means the writer's surname stops short of its final letter

parts.note: to career is to run headlong
Oscar Wilde, the playwright

explanation.surface: An unfinished Academy Award career leads someone to lose it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oscar' suggests the film award or the NATO letter O; here it is the writer.
explanation.definitionFit: To run wild is to behave without restraint, the same uncontrolled frenzy as going berserk.

clue.text: Silly novel 'Four' is at heart only half a book

indicators.note: at heart places the shortened word in the middle of the rearranged letters
novel means new, so the letters are given a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange
taken as written, as letters to rearrange

indicators.note: only half means the second half of the word is thrown away

parts.note: a volume is a book

explanation.surface: A daft novel called Four that is only half-length at its core.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book in the scene but is the anagram signal; the book is a separate word.
explanation.definitionFit: Frivolous behaviour lacks seriousness, so it is light-minded and silly.

clue.text: Heading off for relative release

indicators.note: heading off means the word loses its head, its first letter

parts.note: an auntie is a relative

explanation.surface: Setting off to get a family member freed.
explanation.definitionFit: To untie a knot or a captive is to undo the bonds and set them free.

clue.text: Dash off genuine short

definitions.meaning: first meaning: slang for running away
second meaning: an informal shortening of a word for lawful or authentic

explanation.surface: Quickly writing an authentic short film.
explanation.walkthrough: As two words, LEG IT is British slang for running off; as one, it is short for legitimate.
explanation.definitionFit: Leg it means to run away fast, and legit is a clipped form of legitimate, meaning real.

clue.text: Dream about cry of encouragement abroad leading to resistance

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for a dream goes around the cheer

parts.note: a trance is a dreamlike state
the Spanish cheer at a bullfight

explanation.surface: A daydream about a foreign cheer that inspires defiance.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolerance is the body's resistance to a drug or poison, built up through repeated exposure.

clue.text: Don't be so appreciative — it's unrewarding

definitions.meaning: first meaning, split in two: an instruction to show less gratitude
second meaning: a task that earns no gratitude

explanation.surface: A grumble that showing gratitude gets you nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half reads as two words, THANK LESS, an order to express less gratitude.
explanation.definitionFit: A thankless job is one that brings no recognition or reward for the effort put in.

clue.text: Short book Croatia translated, about performing as a gymnast

indicators.note: translated means turned into another form, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for book
taken as written
C is short for circa, about

explanation.surface: A short Croatian book rendered into English, about a gymnast's routine.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrobatic describes the agile tumbling and balancing feats a gymnast performs.

clue.text: No star fouled a sporting opponent

parts.note: biting an opponent is a notorious foul
a player on the opposing team

explanation.surface: A minor player who committed a foul on a rival.
explanation.walkthrough: Footballers have been banned for biting opponents, so 'fouled' fits the past tense of bite.
explanation.definitionFit: A bit player has only a small part in a film or play, so is certainly not its star.

clue.text: 'God' misspelt as such, after carriage return

indicators.note: after places the rearranged word second, behind the turned-round vehicle
return means going back, so the vehicle is read from the end

parts.note: a cab was a horse-drawn carriage

indicators.note: a misspelt word has its letters in the wrong order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A typist complaining that a word came out wrong after hitting the carriage return key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carriage return' looks like the typewriter key, but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Bacchus is the Roman god of wine, the counterpart of the Greek Dionysus.

clue.text: Is turning up with nothing to cut rent twisting?

indicators.note: cutting into something means going inside it

parts.note: rent as the past participle of rend, ripped

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up means the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A landlord asking whether anything is being done to reduce the rent, or whether it is a twist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' looks like money paid to a landlord, but it means ripped.
explanation.definitionFit: Torsion is the act or state of twisting an object about its axis.

clue.text: Supplier, in quotes, 'Corporation'

indicators.note: in means the letters lie inside the words that follow

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A vendor asking a large company for prices.
explanation.walkthrough: Tesco is Britain's largest supermarket chain.
explanation.definitionFit: Tesco is a retailer that provides groceries and goods to shoppers, a supplier in the everyday sense.

clue.text: See 24
Love, jumpy but not very demanding

indicators.note: the abbreviation for very, a single letter, must be left out

parts.note: love is zero in tennis
jumpy means on edge

explanation.surface: A lover who is anxious but not too needy.
explanation.definitionFit: An onerous task is burdensome and heavy, requiring great effort, hence demanding.

clue.text: Apple disheartened by this device?

parts.note: surface reading: someone saddened by a gadget from the tech company
setter's reading: the kitchen tool literally removes the heart of a fruit

explanation.walkthrough: 'Apple' looks like the tech firm and 'disheartened' like dismayed; read literally, the tool takes out the centre of the fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A corer is a kitchen implement that cuts out the seeded centre of apples and pears.

clue.text: New, albeit fancy, consumers' drink

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or imagined, so the letters are worked into a new pattern

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A trendy new beverage aimed at shoppers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'consumers' are not shoppers but eaters at the meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Table wine is ordinary wine drunk with meals, so it is a drink for diners who are consuming food.

clue.text: Stupid person, American, becomes an emperor

parts.note: British slang for a fool
the United States

explanation.surface: A foolish Yank rises to become ruler of an empire.
explanation.definitionFit: Titus was a Roman emperor of the first century, son of Vespasian.

clue.text: Climatology possibly makes Chinese react badly

indicators.note: badly means done wrongly, so the letters come out in a muddled order

parts.note: the twelve letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Talk of global warming upsets Beijing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' marks the definition as an example rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Climatology, the study of climate, is one branch of the sciences that study the planet.

clue.text: Musical bag, lock container

parts.note: Hair is the 1960s rock musical
to net is to catch or bag

explanation.surface: A theatre bag with a padlock on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lock' is not a padlock but a lock of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairnet is a fine mesh worn to keep locks of hair in place.

clue.text: Hill in position above city

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor
onto means to a position on top of something

explanation.surface: A hilltop overlooking a town.
explanation.definitionFit: Toronto is the largest city in Canada and the capital of Ontario.

clue.text: South, if not cloud-covered

parts.note: S for south
unless means if not

explanation.surface: A weather forecast: the south, if not overcast.
explanation.definitionFit: When the sky is overcast no sunshine gets through, so the day is without sun.

clue.text: Supermarket workers disposing of small notebooks

indicators.note: disposing of means getting rid of the single letter named next

parts.note: staff at the tills
S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: Shop staff throwing away little jotters.
explanation.definitionFit: Cahier is the French word for an exercise book, borrowed into English for a notebook.
